Place value is the value of a digit based on its position in a number. Take the number 3,452. Reading from the right: 2 is in the units place (value 2), 5 is in the tens place (value 50), 4 is in the hundreds place (value 400), and 3 is in the thousands place (value 3,000). So 3,452 means 3,000 + 400 + 50 + 2. The same digit can have different values depending on where it stands, just like the position of a person in a queue at the bank decides who is served first.

To round 4,567 to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit, because it decides whether we round up or down. The hundreds digit is 5 and the tens digit is 6. Since 6 is 5 or more, we round the hundreds up: 5 becomes 6, and the digits after it become zero. So 4,567 rounded to the nearest hundred is 4,600.

LCM means Lowest Common Multiple, the smallest number that both numbers divide into. List the multiples. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24... Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24... The common multiples are 12, 24... and the lowest one is 12. So the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. This is useful in real life, for example to know when two buses that leave every 4 and 6 minutes will leave together again, after 12 minutes.

Why do we write commas in large numbers like 1,000,000?

Good observation! We group the digits in threes from the right and separate the groups with commas to make big numbers easy to read. Without commas, 1000000 is hard to read at a glance. With commas, 1,000,000, you can quickly see it is one million. Each group has a name: the first group is units, the next is thousands, and the next is millions. So the commas act like signposts that tell you which group you are looking at.
